title: The Curled Row, and One Letter from the Lips

lessons.title: ट (ṭa) — the tongue curled back
lessons.gloss: retroflex ta — the tongue curled back to the ridge

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say ta with your tongue on your teeth. Now curl the tip up and back until it touches the ridge behind them, and say it again.
ट (ṭa).

That second sound is ट, ṭa. Marathi has a whole row of these retroflex letters, made with the tongue tip curled back, and they are genuinely different words from the dental row you already write: त and ट are not variants.

The shape is a hook that opens to the right and hangs from the headline. It is the sound in ṭebal, the borrowed word for table, and it is why this book has been writing ṭ with a dot under it in every romanization you have read.
Trace ट (ṭa) twice, then trace त once beside it. Say each one with the tongue in the right place. If they sound the same, the tongue has not moved.
Teeth or ridge for ट (ṭa)? (Ridge.)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari tta stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Trace retroflex ta, then say where the tongue goes for it.
acceptedResponses: ट; curled back to the ridge behind the teeth

feedback.correct: The dot under the romanization now has a shape.
feedback.incorrect: Curl the tongue tip up and back, then trace again.

lessons.title: ठ (ṭha) — the curl, with the breath let out
lessons.gloss: aspirated retroflex ta — the same curl with the breath released

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The four-way pattern again: you have the plain one, so you can predict the next.
ठ (ṭha).

ठ is ṭha: ट (ṭa) with the breath released. You have now seen this step three times — क/ख, च/छ, and here — which is the point. Devanagari is built so that hearing one pair teaches you to expect the rest.
The shape is a plain circle sitting under the headline. It is the roundest letter in the alphabet and the easiest of this chapter to draw.
Copy ठ (ṭha) twice with the model visible. Then write ट (ṭa) once from memory and check the hook did not close into a circle.
Which of the two is a full circle? (ठ (ṭha).)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari ttha stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Copy aspirated retroflex tha, then write plain retroflex ta from memory.

feedback.correct: A circle and a hook, told apart.
feedback.incorrect: Open the hook, or close the circle — repair only one.

lessons.title: ड (ḍa) — the curl, with the voice on
lessons.gloss: retroflex da — the voiced member of the curled row

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Fingers on the throat, tongue curled back. Say ṭa, then switch the voice on.
ड (ḍa).
ड is ḍa, the voiced member of the curled row (vaḷlelī olī) — the same relationship ग has to क.

Marathi needs it for ḍoḷā, "eye", a word that also carries the retroflex ळ you learned in the doorway chapters. Draw the top stroke, then the body that curves down and closes to the left under the headline.
Look at ड (ḍa) for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set it beside ठ (ṭha): one closes into a ring, the other does not.
Which word for a part of the face starts with ड (ḍa)? (ḍoḷā — eye.)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari dda stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Write retroflex da after a delay, then name the plain and aspirated members of its row.

feedback.correct: Three of the curled row, retrieved together.
feedback.incorrect: Repair only the shape, or only the missed name.

lessons.title: ण (ṇa) — the nasal with the tongue curled back
lessons.gloss: retroflex na — the nasal of the curled row, the letter in paani

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Every row in this alphabet ends with its own nasal. The curled row (vaḷlelī olī) is no exception.
ण (ṇa).

ण is ṇa: the tongue curled back, the air through the nose. Set it against न, the dental nasal you learned in your first chapter, and the difference is the same one you made a moment ago for ta and ṭa.

This is the single most useful letter in this chapter. It ends every Marathi infinitive this book teaches — bolṇe, khāṇe, jāṇe, sāṅgṇe — so once it is yours, the shape of "to do something" is readable.
Copy ण (ṇa) twice with the model visible. Then write न once beside it and say both aloud, curling the tongue only for the first.
Which letter ends bolṇe and khāṇe? (ण (ṇa), with the e-mark after it.)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari nna stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Copy retroflex na, then write dental na and say which needs the curled tongue.

feedback.incorrect: Repair only the shape you missed, then say both again.

lessons.title: प (pa) — the lips, with the voice off
lessons.gloss: pa — the lips' plain voiceless stop, partner to the ba you know

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Leave the tongue alone for this one. Close your lips, and let the voice stay off.
प (pa).
प is pa, the voiceless partner of the ब you already write. Same lips, same closure, voice switched off — the fourth time this book has used that one distinction to give you a letter.
It opens pāṇī, "water", and pāhṇe, "to see", and it stands inside punhā, "again", in the goodbye you already say. The shape is ब without the inner dot: left bowl, right stem, headline across.
Look at प for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set it beside ब: the missing dot is the whole difference on the page.
Voice on or off for प (pa)? (Off.)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari pa stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Write pa after a delay, then name the letter it differs from by one dot.

feedback.correct: One dot on the page, one switch in the throat.
feedback.incorrect: Leave the inner dot out for pa.

lessons.title: The curled row (vaḷlelī olī), and one letter from the lips
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the curled row and the plain p, with the earlier marks at distance

segments.text: One question for the row: where is the tongue? Then two older marks, further back than you have retrieved them before.
Tongue curled back: plain, breathy, voiced, nasal. (ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ṇa.)
Which of them ends every infinitive this book teaches? (ṇa.)
Lips closed, voice off — and one dot fewer than ब. (pa.)
Where does the short-i mark go on the page? (Left of its letter.)
One chapter back, at the roof of the mouth: plain, breathy, voiced. (ca, cha, ja.)
Which of those three does Marathi also say as ts? (ca.)

segments.prompt: Name the four curled letters in order, the lip letter that differs from ba by one dot, the two marks from two chapters ago by placement, and the plain, breathy and voiced letters of the palate row.
acceptedResponses: ṭa ṭha ḍa ṇa; pa; i-matra written left, u-matra hung below; ca cha ja

feedback.correct: A whole row, a lip letter, and two marks still holding at distance.
feedback.incorrect: Repair only what was missed; do not re-say the ones that came.
